doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: Wrap-up: parallel life as factory manager and Melody Maker stringer
summary: Vacher describes working in industry while filing Melody Maker reviews overnight; the interview ends with thanks.

story.theme_name: Thanks and goodbyes: closing the interview
story.community_name: Closing thanks and goodbyes at the end of the interview

blocks.x: Well I’m glad there’s guys out there like you doing it.
Well thank you.
I appreciate it.
We’ll try.
It’s been great having this chance to talk to you.
A pleasure, thank you for asking me.
Is there anything that you’d like to wrap up with about what you do?

Well the only thing is that it’s always been a parallel life. I’ve had serious jobs in industry. I mean I was the director of a public company. That was, if you like, how I made my living and paid the bills and raised my family. But there was always this parallel life. And while I was working for the Melody Maker, which I did for about fifteen years, I was always a freelance. I was what is called a stringer. And people found it quite odd that I would go to Ronnie Scott’s to hear Stan Getz — I was managing a factory at that time. And I’d be coming in early to my plant, at eight o’clock in the morning, I’d got home at two o’clock, I’d written 350 words immediately on getting home, and by eight o’clock I was in my office and I was phoning it on to the stone, it was direct to the text taker to go straight down onto the stone. See it printed on a Tuesday. Ronnie Scott’s opens on a Monday. And you know, my boss would sometimes wander in the room when I was doing this. And I’d say I’m sorry I’m doing something important, do you mind getting out? But I think people think it quite interesting, this mad person wishing to pursue these parallel lines. Well for the last thirteen, fourteen years, I haven’t had that problem, I’m a full time freelance now.
Good.
But it made for some funny moments.
All right. Well I hope we cross paths again sometime.
Well I hope so too, it’s been great. And I’m delighted at what you’re doing, you know. Keep it up, sir.
I will.
Okay.
I’ve got the world’s greatest gig.
Yes. I think you have actually. Don’t tell too many people.
I won’t.
Does that have any value or meaning at all?
I think it did.
Was that remotely interesting? Can’t have been. © Fillius Jazz Archive -21-
